title: The Grand Inquisitor
text:
In The Brothers Karamazov, Ivan Karamazov tells his younger brother Alyosha a story he has composed. It is set in Seville in the sixteenth century, at the height of the Inquisition, the day after a hundred heretics have been burned. Christ quietly appears among the people. They recognize him at once, crowd around him, and he heals a blind man and raises a dead child.

The Grand Inquisitor, a cardinal of nearly ninety, sees this and has him arrested. That night the old man visits the prisoner in his cell. He does most of the talking, and Christ says nothing.

The Inquisitor accuses him of having overestimated humanity. In the desert, Christ refused to turn stones into bread, to perform a miracle that would compel belief, and to take the kingdoms of the world. He wanted people to follow him freely. But freedom, says the Inquisitor, is an unbearable burden for most people. They want bread, miracle, mystery and authority. The Church has corrected his work: it has taken their freedom and given them certainty, and the people are grateful. Tomorrow, he says, the crowd will help burn Christ.

When he finishes, the prisoner rises, approaches and silently kisses the old man on his bloodless lips. The Inquisitor shudders, opens the door and tells him to go and never come back.
lesson: Taking decisions away from people can be presented as kindness. Be wary of any authority, including your own, that keeps people comfortable by keeping them from thinking for themselves.
people: The Grand Inquisitor, the prisoner (Christ), Ivan and Alyosha Karamazov
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book V, Chapter 5
